title: M&A Diligence Reports: What Buyers Need to Know Before They Commit
summary: Verify seller claims, rank risks, and get a proceed, proceed-with-conditions, or walk call on power and data center acquisitions in five business days.
body_markdown:
**The short answer:** Before acquiring a power project, powered land, or a data center site, buyers should verify the seller's claims against independent data, find what's missing or expiring, and check what's changed on the grid since the data room was built. Paces M&A Diligence Reports package that work into one recommendation (proceed, proceed with conditions, or walk), backed by a ranked risk register and a diligence request list, in five business days on average.


Buying an existing project has become one of the fastest ways to power. With interconnection queue waits stretching[four to five years](https://emp.lbl.gov/news/backlog-power-plants-seeking-transmission-grid-connection-eased-somewhat-2025-amidst) in CAISO, MISO, and PJM, more data center developers, IPPs, and asset managers are buying their way in rather than starting from scratch.


This M&A trend is showing up in the headlines too.[Altus Power's recent acquisition](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261110225563/en/Altus-Power-Grows-Operating-Solar-and-Battery-Storage-Portfolio-to-1.7-GW-Across-33-States) of 92 operating projects from Arevon is one of a steady run of portfolio deals, as owners choose to grow by buying rather than building.


The catch is that every acquisition starts with a data room the seller assembled, and it's organized to close a deal. Buyers are reviewing more of these rooms than ever, often with only a few weeks to decide.


In the second session of Paces Accelerate, Josh Brown from Paces Solutions Engineering introduced M&A Diligence Reports and demonstrated how buyers can pressure-test a seller's data room and reach a defensible decision in days rather than weeks.

#### **Why M&A Diligence Is a Critical Piece of Smart Investment Strategy**


An approved queue position has become what[FTI Consulting](https://www.fticonsulting.com/en/canada/insights/articles/power-renewables-energy-transition-2025-ma-year-review-2026-outlook) calls “the primary currency in the sector.” That makes acquisitions attractive, and it also raises the stakes on getting diligence right. Buyers tend to run into three challenges:


- **Volume:** Acquisition teams are reviewing more opportunities on tighter timelines. One director of acquisitions Paces works with received nearly 200 data rooms in just three months.
- **Unverified claims:** A data room tells the seller's story. The claims a deal is priced on (site control, acreage, zoning, the serving utility, and available capacity) need to hold up against independent records. In one recent Paces review of a 6-parcel data center campus, the seller didn't own any of the parcels, and there was no lease option or letter of intent in the room.
- **Changing conditions:** Projects can take years to move from interconnection request to commercial operation. A capacity study from early in a project's life may not reflect what's been built, queued, or withdrawn nearby since. In one review of a 1 GW data center site, a Paces Power Flow Study showed that right-sizing the load to 600 MW would cut roughly $120 million in grid upgrades.


The deals look different – a data center campus, a powered land site, a portfolio of solar and storage projects – but they all require due diligence. Before committing capital, buyers need to know what's actually in the deal and what risks they may encounter.


#### **What the M&A Diligence Report Includes**


Paces M&A Diligence Reports give buyers an independent, sourced read on what's in the deal. They cover data center and powered land sites alongside solar and storage projects, before NTP and COD.


Every review starts with a scoping call on deal context, so our team is aligned with yours on strategy and priorities. Paces uses AI to parse the data room, then our energy and data center experts verify each finding against external research. Each review works through more than 175 diligence items and records the evidence (or its absence) for every one.


Each report includes:


**1. Recommendation**
A clear call to proceed, proceed with conditions, or walk, with a summary of the findings that drive it.


**2. Seller Claims vs. the Record**
The claims a deal is priced on, including acreage, buildable area, zoning, site control, the serving utility, and capacity, checked against independent sources such as county parcel and zoning records, FEMA flood maps, wetland and soil data, service territory maps, and the ISO base case or hosting capacity maps. Each contradiction shows what the seller says, what the record shows, and the source. Where the data can't confirm or rule out a claim, Paces flags it and lists what's needed.


**3. Ranked Risks**
Every risk, ranked by severity, with a path to resolve it. On an early-stage site, this matters more than the percentage of items completed, since many documents simply can't exist yet.


**4. Gaps and Document Currency**
What the room doesn't cover, from missing signed leases and referenced studies to unaddressed risks like water supply or fiber redundancy. Paces also checks each document against its own shelf life and flags anything that needs to be revalidated before close.


**5. Conditions Precedent**
The items to negotiate before close, so findings carry straight into the deal terms.


**6. Diligence Request List**
Every open item tracked as provided in full, in part, missing, or not applicable, with a severity rating and the action needed to resolve it. Buyers can send it straight back to the seller.

#### **Frequently Asked Questions**


**What should buyers check in a seller's data room?**


Start with four questions. Can you verify the seller's claims? What's missing? What's expiring? And what's changed since the room was built? Our[guide to reading a seller's data room](https://www.paces.com/post/buying-a-power-project-heres-how-to-read-the-sellers-data-room) walks through each one.


**How long does an M&A Diligence Report take?**


Five business days on average, from data room access to findings.


**What types of projects does the report cover?**


Data center sites, powered land, and solar and storage projects, including portfolios, before NTP and COD. For community solar and other program-dependent projects, the review also confirms the project still qualifies under current program rules, adders, and deadlines.


**How do M&A Diligence Reports differ from using AI to parse a data room or hiring a consultant?**


A general AI tool can read documents and check public data like flood maps, but it doesn't have Paces' proprietary datasets, such as interconnection withdrawal heat maps and county permitting data, or experts verifying each finding. Consultants bring deep expertise but typically take two to six weeks. Paces M&A Diligence Reports combine both: every finding is verified by Paces energy and data center experts, with a recommendation delivered in five business days on average.


**What if the data room is incomplete or the project is early stage?**


The report records the absence of evidence as a finding. Missing items go on the diligence request list with a severity rating, and on early-stage sites the recommendation leans on the ranked risks rather than the share of documents provided.


**Does the review account for information that isn't in the data room?**


Yes. When a broker call or utility conversation updates the picture, Paces works that context into the review, so a verbal update isn't lost behind an outdated document.
